rungs.stem: In the darkest ballad of the Robin Hood cycle, a fearsome bounty hunter comes stalking through Sherwood to kill Robin for the price on his head. He wears a whole animal's hide as a cloak -- head and tail still attached -- to make himself terrifying. From which ANIMAL is his hide-cloak made?
rungs.context: Stanza 7 of Child Ballad 118 'Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne': 'A sword and a dagger he wore by his side / Had beene many a mans bane / And he was cladd in his capull-hyde / Topp, and tayle, and mayne.' 'Capull-hyde' is Middle English for horse-hide. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.

rungs.stem: The horse-hide-clad bounty hunter of Child Ballad 118 has not come to Sherwood for adventure -- he has been HIRED by a powerful enemy of Robin's to collect the bounty on the outlaw's head. Who has hired the hunter?
rungs.context: In the ballad the Sheriff of Nottingham is at once hunting Robin's men in the forest and has commissioned Guy to hunt Robin himself; the Sheriff and Guy meet in the wood while Guy is on his errand. The Bishop of Hereford, the Abbot of St Mary's, and the Prioress of Kirklees are all real enemies of Robin from other ballads. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood_and_Guy_of_Gisborne.

rungs.stem: Robin and Little John have QUARRELLED and gone their separate ways in the wood. Robin, alone, meets the hunter in the horse-hide cloak, not knowing who he is. The two men fight -- for two hours of a summer's day, the ballad says. With what WEAPONS do they fight?
rungs.context: Stanzas 33-38 of the ballad: 'To see how together these yeomen went / With blades both browne and bright / To see how they hewed on eche other / It was a wonderous fight.' The fight is with 'blades' -- swords. The bow-shot in this ballad is only an earlier target-shooting contest, not the killing fight. Source: traditionalmusic.co.uk/child-ballads/ch118.htm.

rungs.stem: Late in the sword-fight Robin STUMBLES ON A ROOT and falls; the hunter stands over him with the blade raised. In that moment of danger Robin cries out a prayer to a heavenly figure -- 'Ah, deere Lady! ... Thou art both mother and may!' To WHOM is Robin praying?
rungs.context: Stanza 39: 'Ah, deere Lady! sayd Robin Hoode / Thou art both mother and may! / I thinke it was neuer mans destinye / To dye before his day.' 'May' is Middle English for maiden -- the 'mother and maiden' address is Marian, and stanza 40 continues 'Robin thought on Our Lady deere / And soone leapt vp againe.' Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.

rungs.stem: Recovering from his stumble, Robin kills the hunter with 'an awkwarde stroke' and then does something shocking with the corpse. Stanza 41: 'He tooke Sir Guys head by the hayre / And sticked itt on his...' -- on WHAT does Robin fix the severed head?
rungs.context: 'He tooke Sir Guys head by the hayre / And sticked itt on his bowes end.' Robin walks with the head raised on his own longbow like a standard. It is one of the grimmest single images in any Robin Hood ballad. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.

rungs.stem: Not content with the beheading, Robin then draws a KNIFE and slashes at the dead hunter's face until 'hee was neuer on a woman borne / Cold tell who Sir Guy was' -- ruined past recognition. What KIND of knife does the ballad say Robin draws?
rungs.context: Stanza 42: 'Robin pulled forth an Irish kniffe / And nicked Sir Guy in the face.' Irish knives -- long, single-edged blades of Gaelic manufacture -- circulated in the English borderlands and had a reputation for cruel work; the ballad specifies the kind. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.

rungs.stem: Robin then strips the horse-hide from the dead hunter and pulls it on over his own body. What does he do with his OWN Lincoln-green gown after taking it off?
choices: throws it over the hunter's corpse
hangs it on the branch of an oak
buries it under a heap of leaves
carries it rolled up under his arm
rungs.answer: throws it over the hunter's corpse
rungs.context: Stanza 44: 'Robin did off his gowne of greene / Sir Guye hee did it throwe / And hee put on that capull-hyde / That cladd him topp to toe.' The disguise-swap is total: Robin becomes the horse-hide hunter and the hunter is dressed as Robin. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.

rungs.stem: Wearing the horse-hide, Robin walks out of the trees toward the Sheriff of Nottingham -- who thinks the hunter he hired is coming to report the kill. Robin fools him with a signal the Sheriff has been waiting for. What SIGNAL does the disguised Robin give?
choices: he blows the hunter's hunting horn
he waves the hunter's Lincoln bow
he holds up a green rag on a stick
rungs.answer: he blows the hunter's hunting horn
rungs.context: Stanza 46: 'Robin sett Guyes horne to his mouth / A lowd blast in it he did blow.' The Sheriff hears Guy's own horn and rides toward it thinking Guy has won -- and Robin is waiting. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.

rungs.stem: Meanwhile the Sheriff has captured LITTLE JOHN in the woods, away from Robin. In the ballad the Sheriff's men do a very specific thing to Little John while they wait for the hunter's kill -- stanza 19 says 'they haue tane Litle Iohn / And bound him fast to a...'. Bound him fast to a WHAT?
rungs.context: Stanza 19 of Child 118: 'And they haue tane Litle Iohn / And bound him fast to a tree.' The point is grim symmetry -- the Sheriff wants to hang Little John from that tree once Robin is confirmed dead. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.

rungs.stem: Robin cuts Little John's ropes with the Irish knife and hands him the hunter's own weapon to finish the ambush. Little John looses one arrow at the fleeing Sheriff and, in the ballad's line, 'with an arrow broade / Did cleaue his heart in twinn.' Which weapon does Little John use for that killing shot?
choices: a peasant's hunting bow from a hut
rungs.context: The point of the ballad's poetic justice: the hunter's own bow finishes the hunter's employer. Stanza 58: 'But Litle Iohn, with an arrow broade / Did cleaue his heart in twinn.' The Sheriff dies with the hunter's arrow in him. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.

rungs.stem: This is by far the DARKEST surviving ballad of the Robin Hood cycle -- the beheading, the knife-slashing of the face, and Robin wearing a dead man's skin do not appear in any of the sanitised modern retellings. The ballad survives in only ONE seventeenth-century English manuscript. In WHICH manuscript is Child 118 preserved?
rungs.context: The Percy Folio is the c. 1650 English manuscript of ballads and romances discovered by Bishop Thomas Percy in the 1750s; Child 118 survives only there, though the story is clearly much older (a related dramatic fragment is dated c. 1475). The Vernon and Auchinleck manuscripts are older but hold different romance material; Cotton Nero A.x holds 'Sir Gawain and the Green Knight'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood_and_Guy_of_Gisborne.
